Forecast Uncertainty & Ensembles

Why good forecasters embrace being wrong
45 min · Business & Engineering · OpenWeather
02 · The problem

The single-forecast problem

A single line looks authoritative — but it's just one draw from a range of plausible futures. Toggle the ensemble on and off to see what a lone forecast conceals.

  • A single forecast looks certain — but hides the range of what could happen.
  • Two runs can agree today and diverge sharply a few days out.
  • Small errors grow fast — the limit is fundamental, not a flaw.

Comment: the coral line is the same member in both views. Alone it implies false precision; inside the cloud you can read the real spread.

T+7
03 · Where it comes from

Initial condition and model error

Spread has two roots: imperfect knowledge of today's state (IC error) and model approximations (model error). Dial each to see how it contributes.

Initial condition errors
Observation limits · instrumental noise · spatial/temporal gaps · data-assimilation uncertainty.
Model errors
Numerical approximations · discretization limits · sub-grid parametrizations · simplified equations.

Comment: IC error dominates early; model error accumulates with lead time.

04 · The physics

Chaos and error growth

The atmosphere is chaotic: two states that start almost identical drift apart exponentially. Shrink the initial error all you like — it only buys you a little more lead time before forecasts diverge.

  • Tiny differences in starting conditions grow exponentially.
  • Beyond ~2 weeks, individual forecasts lose all skill.
  • A range of outcomes is always the honest answer.

Comment: halving the initial error pushes the predictability horizon out by only a fixed amount — the curve just shifts right.

05 · The fix

The ensemble distribution

Launch many runs from slightly different starts. Sliced at any lead time, the members form a distribution. Slide T+ to see how the PDF evolves.

  • Run the model many times from slightly different starting points.
  • Each run is a plausible scenario — together they form a distribution.
  • Read percentiles and exceedance probabilities from that distribution.
The textbook picture — initial-condition uncertainty fanning into a forecast distribution (Met Office).

06 · How it's done

Initial condition perturbations

Perturb along directions the atmosphere is most sensitive to. A handful of members then efficiently spans the range of where the forecast can go. Left: perturbed starts. Right: resulting spread.

  • Perturb the starting state along directions most likely to cause divergence.
  • Also vary model physics to sample model uncertainty.
  • Each scenario stays physically self-consistent.
  • Singular Vectors (SVs) — directions of maximum error growth over a finite window. Used by ECMWF ENS, combined with the Ensemble of Data Assimilations (EDA).
  • Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (ETKF) — propagates analysis uncertainty directly from data assimilation. Used by the UK Met Office MOGREPS.
  • Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) — members drawn from the operational EnKF analysis ensemble. Used by NCEP GEFS and Canada's GEPS.
  • Stochastic physics (SPPT/SKEB) — random perturbations to parameterized tendencies and kinetic energy, layered on top of IC perturbations. Used by ECMWF, NCEP, and most operational centres.

Comment: targeted perturbations line up along the growing direction (dashed). The same number of members then fans into a far wider, more useful forecast spread than random nudges.

Initial states at T+0 (perturbations around the analysis)
Forecast spread they produce later
07 · Multi-model

Multi-model ensembles

Each model carries its own bias. Combined, they partly cancel — the multi-model mean usually beats any single model. Toggle models to see.

Independent models make different mistakes. Averaging them cancels part of each one's bias — the classic free lunch of multi-model ensembles.

Comment: each colour is one model's members and mean. The thick dark line is the combined mean; the black line is the verifying truth. Turn models off and the combined line drifts away.

ECMWF GFS ICON Combined Truth
08 · The trap

Bimodal distributions

When members split into two scenarios, the distribution is bimodal. The mean lands in the empty valley — a value almost no member predicts. Pull the scenarios apart to see every summary statistic fail.

A bimodal ensemble is the textbook trap: the mean sits where nothing happens, and even the median can fall in the gap. The real forecast is "two outcomes, ~50/50".

Comment: watch the coral mean line drop into the valley as separation grows. Reporting any single number here hides the actual decision.

Mean Median P10 / P25 / P75 / P90

10 · Reading spread

Spread as a confidence signal

Same model, different days. Calm day → tight spread, high confidence. Volatile day → wide spread — there the distribution is the forecast. Switch between the two.

  • Narrow spread → scenarios agree → high confidence.
  • Wide spread → scenarios diverge → the distribution is the forecast.
  • Wide spread reflects real uncertainty — information, not failure.

Comment: the trajectories on the left and the PDF on the right are the same data. The spread is a feature to act on, not a quality score to minimise.

11 · Trust

Reliability: do stated odds verify?

Plot claimed probability vs observed frequency. Perfect calibration = diagonal. Overconfident model produces an S-shape squeezed toward 50%: above the line at low probabilities, below at high ones. Teal (calibrated) lands on the line.

  • "30% chance of rain" should rain ~30% of the time — no more, no less.
  • Overconfidence = too extreme. Model says 10% when true odds are 30% → point is above diagonal. Model says 90% when true odds are 70% → point is below diagonal.
  • In both cases the curve is squeezed toward 50%: the model uses probabilities closer to the extremes than the data supports.
  • Teal (calibrated): post-processed. Stated odds match observed frequency — on the diagonal.
  • Sampling noise dominates with few cases — need thousands to see the true shape reliably.

Comment: the S-shape is overconfidence. The model thinks it knows more than it does — spreads probabilities toward 0% and 100%. Calibration compresses them back toward what the data actually supports.

12 · The calibration step

Shift, rescale, extract

Each coral dot is a past observation. The raw ensemble PDF (gray) sits in the wrong place and is too narrow — watch how many dots fall outside its range. Calibration shifts by bias and inflates spread by α until the teal distribution covers the observations ~80% of the time.

  • Coral dots — what actually happened on many past forecast days. Their scatter is the real uncertainty the forecast should match.
  • Raw PDF (gray) — centered at 0, but the dots cluster to the right (bias) and spill outside its range (too narrow). It claims more certainty than it earns.
  • Bias — horizontal shift that re-centers the distribution onto where the observations actually land.
  • α — spread inflation: σcal = α × σraw. α > 1 widens the over-confident raw spread.
  • P10 / P50 / P90 — read off the calibrated curve. Goal: P10–P90 holds ~80% of the dots.

Comment: read the coverage pills. The raw band holds only ~40% of past observations — far short of 80%. Drag bias toward +0.7 and α toward ~1.8 and the teal band finally covers four-fifths of the dots.

13 · Learning α from data

Training the calibration

Collect (raw forecast, observation) pairs from a training archive. Fit the mapping — the residual spread tells you α. More samples → more stable estimate. Switch to ML fit to capture non-linear model errors.

  • Need a long training archive: same location, same lead time, same model version.
  • Linear (MOS): fast, interpretable, handles most systematic biases. Still operational at NWS/NOAA.
  • ML (EMOS/QRF): captures curved relationships — but needs more samples to be stable.
  • α from residuals: after fitting the mean correction, measure the residual spread σres. Then α = σres / σraw.
  • α is re-estimated every model cycle — model upgrades shift it.

Comment: tight scatter around the fit line = low residual error = smaller α needed. Wide scatter = large unexplained variance = α must be large. Fewer samples makes α noisy.

40
14 · One score

CRPS

CRPS measures the gap between the forecast CDF (teal) and a perfect step at the observation. A good forecast must be both on-target (centred) and sharp (tight grouping) — CRPS is the single score that rewards both at once. The shaded lens is that gap — it shrinks as you centre and tighten, grows when you over-hedge. Lower is better.

  • Rewards forecasts that are sharp and reliable — can't be gamed by hedging.
  • Measures how far the full distribution is from the observed outcome.
  • Bias = 0 and spread → 0 (a sharp spike on the observation) gives CRPS ≈ 0.

Comment: the shaded lens shows the gap for intuition; the score itself sums it squared — ∫(F−H)² — so larger misses cost disproportionately more. "Bias" is the offset from the observed value, so at zero bias, tightening the spread drives CRPS toward zero.

15 · Spread-skill

Spread–skill relationship

Wide-spread days should be harder to forecast; narrow-spread days should be accurate. Spread-skill check: does spread actually correlate with error? Tune from noise to a clean relationship.

  • Wide scenarios should predict large errors — and vice versa.
  • A spread-skill check confirms whether spread reliably signals confidence.
  • Too-narrow spread creates false certainty — more dangerous than admitting doubt.

Comment: lined up along the diagonal, spread is trustworthy. A shapeless blob means spread tells you nothing about the error.

16 · Across timescales

Nowcast to seasonal

Same probabilistic machinery, minutes to months — only the source of skill shifts. Short range: atmospheric dynamics. Long range: ocean and land memory. Slide lead time to see the handover.

  • One probabilistic framework spans minutes to seasons.
  • Short range: the atmosphere is predictable; long range: ocean and land carry the signal.
  • Modern coupled models give consistent probabilities from day 1 to month 3.

Comment: where teal hands off to blue is the regime change — and why a seasonal forecast is still a real, if humbler, forecast.

17 · Recap

Three things to remember

The whole talk in three ideas — each with a live reminder.

1

Uncertainty is physical

The atmosphere is chaotic. Spread is genuine information about the range of plausible outcomes — not a model failure.

2

Ensemble = distribution

Read percentiles and exceedance probabilities, not just the mean. Tail scenarios represent real risk.

3

Trust the probabilities

Check calibration before you act on a probability. Reliable odds are the foundation of good decisions.

18 · Why it matters

From one number to odds you can act on

For decades a forecast meant a single number. An ensemble gives a fan of outcomes that widens with lead time. Drag the day to read the odds — the median, the 50% and 80% ranges, and the value with only a 10% chance of being exceeded.

  • Decide under risk. Act on the probability of crossing a threshold versus your tolerance — not on a single point guess.
  • Speak in confidence. "Expect ~10°, 80% chance 7–13°, could reach 15°" beats false-precision "10°".
  • Edge over deterministic. Priced risk means better margins and fewer surprises than single-number competitors.

Same forecast, richer decision. The point estimate is still there — it's just the peak of a distribution you can now hedge against.

Temperature fan — the range of outcomes widens with lead time
